paras: The killing of Charles Haynes was the fatal shooting of Haynes, a Black man, by the attorney B. W. Moore at McKenzie, Tennessee, in late July 1880. Haynes died of the wound, and Moore was reported both to have surrendered and to have "left the country." The quarrel grew out of Haynes's interruption of Moore's speech at a barbecue.

A few days before the shooting, Moore spoke at a barbecue in Weakley County, and Haynes interrupted his speech. Haynes had also threatened Moore's life, according to the Nashville dispatch, a claim the Milan Exchange repeated with the hedge "we learn."

When the two men met at McKenzie on "Wednesday of last week," about July 28, Moore spoke to Haynes about the interruption, and Haynes took hold of Moore's stick. Moore ordered him to let it go, warning in the Exchange's version that he would shoot, and after a short struggle he fired, hitting Haynes in the abdomen.

The first dispatch said Haynes was mortally wounded and that Moore "gave himself up." A postscript in the Milan Exchange added that Haynes had died and that Moore had left. No report of an inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The Dallas Daily Herald printed the Nashville dispatch on August 1 as "Negro Killed," giving only Moore's account and closing with "Haynes is a turbulent character." The Milan Exchange's "Carroll Items" column of August 5 called the shooting a "difficulty" and Haynes "a desperate man." The National Republican reduced the case to one sentence in its "Political Notes," saying Moore "treasured up the wrong" before shooting "the African."

Accounts differ on whether Moore surrendered or left, and on whether the shooting came the "next-day" after the speech or a few days later. The same Milan page also reprinted a Huntingdon Vindicator item saying that "Custer, the man who shot and killed the negro at McKenzie last week," had not been captured and that "Both were Republicans." That item names no victim, and the coverage does not show whether "Custer" was a garbled name for Moore or a different man.

reader.title: Killing of Charles Haynes
bases: One man, the attorney B. W. Moore, shot Haynes during a personal confrontation over an interrupted speech; no mob, band, posse or officers took part (A1, A2, A3).

The Nashville dispatch (A1) and the separately worded local account in the Milan Exchange (A3) agree that Moore shot Haynes after a speech interruption and a struggle over a stick, and A2 agrees on the core; all three, however, carry only the shooter's side.

accounts.label: Nashville American's McKenzie correspondent (wire)
accounts.gist: Haynes interrupted Moore's barbecue speech and threatened his life; when Moore spoke to him, Haynes seized and wrenched away Moore's stick, and Moore shot him, then gave himself up.

accounts.label: Milan Exchange local column
accounts.gist: Same sequence, with the threat given as hearsay ('we learn'), Moore warning he would shoot, a short struggle, a wound in the abdomen, Hayes's death, and Moore leaving the country.

accounts.label: National Republican note
accounts.gist: Moore 'treasured up the wrong' of the interruption, met the man the next day, and shot him fatally in an altercation.

accounts.label: Huntingdon Vindicator (reprinted)
accounts.gist: A man named Custer shot and killed the negro at McKenzie and had not been captured; both men were Republicans.

framing.detail: The Dallas Daily Herald ran the Nashville dispatch under 'Negro Killed', giving only Moore's account and ending 'Haynes is a turbulent character.'
The Milan Exchange called the shooting a 'difficulty', hedged the threat with 'we learn', but said Hayes 'had the reputation of being a desperate man.'
The National Republican filed it among 'Political Notes', calling Haynes 'the African' and saying Moore 'treasured up the wrong' before shooting him.

versions.value: Moore left the country after Haynes died
'Custer', the shooter, has not been captured

conflicts.note: A1 is the earliest dispatch; A3's postscript was written later and is local, so Moore may have surrendered and then left, but no paper says so.
The Custer item names no victim; it is unclear whether it is a garbled name for Moore or a second killing at McKenzie.
The two fuller accounts agree on 'a few days'; A2 is a one-sentence summary.

info: Shooting on 'Wednesday of last week' relative to the Thursday, Aug. 5 issue, i.e. about July 28, 1880; first dispatch dated Nashville, July 31
M'Kenzie (McKenzie), Tennessee; the interrupted speech was at a barbecue in Weakley county a few days earlier
No crime charged; the shooter's side said Haynes had interrupted Moore's speech, boasted of it, threatened Moore's life, and seized a stick from him
B. W. Moore, an attorney ('Esq.'); his race is not stated
1 (Haynes, first reported mortally wounded, later reported dead)
